title: Syllables
keyIdea: A syllable is one beat in a spoken word. Cat has one beat, rab-bit has two and but-ter-fly has three. You can clap the beats, glue beats together to make a word, and split a written word into its beats to help you read and spell it. Count beats by listening, not by counting letters: strong has six letters but only one beat.

kid: Words have beats. Say cat. Clap one time. Cat has one beat.
Say rab-bit. Clap two times. Rab-bit has two beats. A beat is called a syllable.
Some long words have one beat. Strong has lots of letters. Say it. Clap one time!
You can glue beats. Rain and bow make rainbow. You can cut a word too: rab and bit.
adult: A syllable is a beat of sound in a spoken word, built around one vowel sound. Counting, blending and splitting syllables is an early step in hearing the sound structure of words, before and alongside phonics. It helps children read longer words in chunks and spell them part by part (the English national curriculum asks Year 1 children to divide words such as rabbit, carrot, thunder and sunset into syllables).

In the lab, your child claps words such as cat, rabbit and butterfly, then compares strong with banana (six letters each, one beat against three). They glue spoken parts into rainbow, popcorn and dinosaur, chop written words at the beat breaks, and sort pictures into one, two or three beats.

Common mistakes: counting letters instead of beats, counting every vowel letter (cake has a and e but one beat, because the final e is silent), and rushing so two beats blur into one. A useful trick is to put a hand under the chin and say the word slowly: the chin drops once for each beat.
Clap names at home. Your child's name, a sibling's, the dog's: how many beats? Then say a word in beats, such as ta-ble, and let them glue it back together.

familyTip: Play a clapping name game: clap each family member's name, one clap per beat (Sam, Ma-ya, Ol-i-ver). Then say a word in parts, like rain ... bow, and ask your child to say the whole word.

practice.prompt: Say butterfly slowly and clap. How many beats?
practice.hint: Say it in parts: but, then ter, then fly. Clap for each part.
practice.explain: But-ter-fly has three parts, so it has 3 beats (syllables). Nine is the number of letters, not beats.

practice.prompt: Kit claps {n} times for cat. Is that right?
practice.hint: Say cat. Do you say it in one go, or in parts?
practice.explain: Cat is said in one go, so it has 1 beat. Its three letters do not make three beats.

practice.prompt: What word do rain and bow make?
practice.hint: Say the parts in order: first rain, then bow, quickly.
practice.explain: Gluing (blending) rain + bow in order makes rainbow. The order matters: bowrain is not a word.

practice.prompt: Sam claps two-beat words, like rab-bit. He claps {n} words. Which word could be next?
practice.hint: Clap each word. Which one has two claps, like rab-bit?
practice.explain: Pen-cil has two beats, like rab-bit. Dog has one beat and but-ter-fly has three.

practice.prompt: Where does carrot break into beats?
practice.hint: Say carrot slowly. What do you hear first?
practice.explain: You say car, then rot, so the beats are car | rot. Each piece has one vowel sound.

pool.hint: Say it slowly: el, e, phant. Clap each part.
pool.explain: El-e-phant has 3 beats. Eight is how many letters it has, which is not the same.

pool.prompt: Strong has 6 letters. How many beats does it have?
pool.hint: Say strong. Do you need to stop in the middle?
pool.explain: Strong is said in one go, so it has 1 beat, even though it has 6 letters.

pool.prompt: Cake has the letters a and e. How many beats?
pool.hint: Say cake. Is the e at the end loud or quiet?
pool.explain: The e at the end of cake is silent, so there is only one vowel sound and 1 beat.

pool.prompt: What word do pop and corn make?
pool.hint: Say first pop, then corn, quickly together.
pool.explain: Pop + corn in that order makes popcorn. Gluing beats in the order you hear them builds the word.

pool.prompt: Where does thunder break into beats?
pool.hint: Say it slowly and listen for where your voice stops for a moment.
pool.explain: You hear thun, then der, so thunder splits as thun | der, with one vowel sound in each piece.

pool.prompt: Mia says ba-na-na and claps {n} times. She says banana has {n} beats. Is she right?
pool.hint: Say ba-na-na and count the parts on your fingers.
pool.explain: Ba-na-na has three parts, so it has 3 beats. Six is the number of letters.

pool.prompt: Ben has {n} picture cards. He wants one with 1 beat, like dog. Which card?
pool.hint: Clap each word. Which one needs only one clap?
pool.explain: Train is said in one go, so it has 1 beat. Ti-ger and ap-ple have two beats each.

pool.hint: Say it slowly: cat, er, pil, lar.
pool.explain: Cat-er-pil-lar has 4 beats. Eleven is the number of letters, not beats.

visual.caption: One beat or two? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: clap the beats, find that letters are not beats, glue parts into words, chop written words at the beats, then sort pictures by beats.
